title: Mongoose schema methods
idea: A schema method is a function you attach to `userSchema.methods`. Every document of that model can call it, and `this` inside it is that document.
points: Assign a function to `userSchema.methods.name`, then build the model.
A method reads the document's own fields, such as `this.password`.
`isPasswordCorrect` hands a plain attempt and the stored hash to `bcrypt.compare`.
Later pages add the token methods the same way.

hero.title: Where a function lives

right.title: Static: lives on the model
items: Works with no document in hand

hero.verdict: Needs one document's fields? Write a method. This project only needs methods.

code.title: src/models/user.models.js
code.caption: The pre-save hook is left out, so the snippet hashes by hand. Step through, then press Run.

walk.text: Assign a regular `function` to `userSchema.methods`, before the model is built.
`this.password` is the stored hash. `compare` checks a plain attempt against it.
`mongoose.model` builds the model from the schema, methods included.
Create a user with a hashed password.
`findOne` returns a document, and every document carries the method.
Call it on the document. It answers `true` or `false`.
The model has no such function, so the type is `undefined`.

pitfalls: Write methods with `function`, not an arrow: arrows do not bind `this`.
Add methods before `mongoose.model()`; methods added to the schema later are ignored.
`.lean()` returns plain objects with no methods; `select('-password')` leaves `this.password` empty.

quiz.q: A document `user` came from `User.findOne`. What does this print?
quiz.why: A method lives on documents, not on the model. The model has no `isPasswordCorrect`, so its type is `undefined`.

takeaway: Methods give every document its own behavior, with `this` as the document.

starters: When would I use a static instead of a method?
Why do methods need a regular function and not an arrow?
